vignette:
Raj was seventy-nine years old when he finally walked into the clinic, a thick-bodied man with silver stubble and hands that still looked strong even after decades of lifting boxes in the warehouse. He had come on his own, after his daughter - the only one of his three children who still spoke to him - had told him plainly that she could not watch him "shrink away" any longer. He sat on the edge of the chair, his back straight, his eyes fixed on a spot on the wall, and he said nothing for a long time. Then, in a voice that sounded as though it had not been used for stories in many years, he began.

He had been a young man in 1968, a recent immigrant from a small village in Punjab, when the draft letter arrived. Within months he was in the Central Highlands of Vietnam, a rifleman in a company that walked through elephant grass and rubber plantations. He remembered a particular afternoon in March, the heat so thick it felt like walking through wet cloth, when his squad entered a village that was supposed to be empty. They had been told to clear it. What Raj remembered most vividly was not the firing, not the shouting, but the moment afterward: standing in the middle of a dirt road, the thatched huts burning on either side, and seeing the body of a woman holding a child who was no longer moving. He had stood there, frozen, as a sergeant yelled at him to move. He did not fire that day - he had been on flank security and arrived after the worst was over - but he had seen. And what he saw had settled into him like a stone.

After the war, Raj returned to the United States, found work at a loading dock, married a woman from his own community, had children. He did not speak about Vietnam. When his wife asked about the nightmares, he said they were nothing. When he jerked awake at three in the morning, sweating, he went to the bathroom and stared at his face in the mirror until his heart slowed. He learned to keep the memories in a locked room inside his head. For decades, that worked. He raised his children, paid his bills, retired at sixty-five from the warehouse, and then, because he could not sit still, went back to work part-time as a greeter and stock clerk. The physical exhaustion helped him sleep.

But the lock on that room had grown old. In the past three years, he had found himself unable to walk past certain things. The smell of cooking meat - especially if it was slightly burnt - made his stomach turn and his throat tighten. The sound of a helicopter on the news, even a traffic helicopter, sent a chill across his scalp. He had stopped visiting his children because one of them lived near a small airport, and the distant drone of engines would leave him restless for hours. He never told them why. They assumed he was becoming difficult in old age.

At the warehouse, his supervisor had noticed that Raj flinched whenever a pallet jack screeched against concrete, and that he avoided the loading bay on days when the truck engines idled in a certain low rumble. Raj had learned to time his breaks to avoid those sounds, but it meant he ate lunch alone in a supply closet, the door shut, the lights off. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel the fear fully, it would never stop - that he would be pulled back into that afternoon in the village and never return. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the certainty that he could not survive it again.

His divorce, twenty years ago, had been quiet and legal, and he had not remarried. His ex-wife had once told him, in a rare moment of honesty, that he had been "gone" since before their first son was born. Raj had not understood what she meant then, but now he thought he did. He had been standing in a burning village for fifty years. The rest of his life had happened around that standing.

He came to the clinic because his daughter had found him crying in the kitchen one morning, staring at a pan he had set on the stove. He had not known he was crying. He had not known he was cold. She had sat him down, held his hand, and said, "It's time, Papa." He had nodded, and the next day he made the appointment.

On the assessment, his PCL-5 score was 65. He answered the questions without hesitation, as though he had been waiting for someone to ask them. When the clinician asked what he hoped for, Raj paused, then said, "I want to be able to sit in a room with my grandchildren without checking the door every few minutes." He did not add that he wanted to sleep, or to stop dreaming, or to feel safe. Those seemed like wishes for another man. But he said it plainly, and the clinician wrote it down.
